page_hint: Ch 9 §6
quoted_clause: about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case
observed: '11× below' and '180× below' are ambiguous phrasings. 'X× below' is not standard mathematical English and could be misread.
evidence: The intended meaning is that the NVLink ring time is ~1/11th of the InfiniBand time and ~1/180th of the RoCE time (0.54 s vs 6.1 s vs 98 s). 6.1/0.54 ≈ 11.3, 98/0.54 ≈ 181.5.

page_hint: Appendix A, 'The Signal in One Paragraph'
quoted_clause: Four 2026 frontier open models we surveyed converge on a **second-order architectural pattern**, which we read as an interpretation rather than an established historical fact.
observed: 'Second-order architectural pattern' is never defined and does not correspond to anything the appendix later names. The appendix's actual thesis — stated two paragraphs later — is a two-ledger split (efficiency vs capability), and the appendix elsewhere argues that architecture is not the dominant lever, which sits awkwardly with 'converge on a ... architectural pattern' as the headline finding.

root_cause: A rhetorical phrase was used where the appendix's own two-ledger framing was available and precise.
correction: Replace with the ledger framing the appendix actually uses ('converge on a shared efficiency playbook — attention re-architecture plus extreme MoE sparsity'), or define 'second-order' explicitly in one clause.

page_hint: Ch 10 §3, Tensor Parallelism subsection (formula and the 160-call example)
quoted_clause: the bandwidth term is $T_\text{tp} \approx n_\text{layers} \times 2(N-1)/N \times M_\text{act}/B_\text{dir}$ ... (The bandwidth term above counts one collective per layer; this budget's two-per-block assumption is why the call count below is 160 rather than 80.)
observed: The general formula is written in terms of n_layers, but the common transformer block issues two collectives (attention output and MLP). The example then silently corrects the formula by using 160 calls, and the correction is relegated to a parenthetical. A reader who applies the formula as written underestimates TP byte traffic by 2× for the canonical 80-layer model — a factor-of-two error in the chapter's central TP budget.
evidence: Recomputation: formula as written gives 80 × 1.75 × 256 KiB = 35 MiB per rank per step → 0.0816 ms at 450 GB/s; the example's 160 calls give 70 MiB → 0.163 ms. The printed 0.163 ms is correct for the example; the printed formula is not the formula that produced it.
root_cause: The formula was written for a one-collective-per-layer abstraction and the example was later specified with two collectives per block; the mismatch was patched in prose rather than in the formula.
correction: Replace n_layers with n_collectives (or n_layers × c where c is the collectives per block, c ≈ 2 for attention+MLP), define c explicitly, and state the assumption inline: 'T_tp ≈ n_collectives × 2(N−1)/N × M_act/B_dir, with n_collectives = c × n_layers and c ≈ 2 for a standard attention+MLP block'. Then the example's 160 follows directly and the parenthetical can be deleted.
acceptance_test: Substituting the example's own inputs into the printed formula reproduces the printed 70 MiB / 0.163 ms; the symbol n_layers no longer appears in a byte-budget formula without a collectives-per-layer multiplier.

page_hint: Ch 10, §3 Worked Example, Pipeline Parallelism subsection, paragraph after the speedup formula
quoted_clause: the P−1 term in the denominator is the bubble: the pipeline fills and drains exactly once per m-batch pass, so P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots each stage would otherwise work
observed: The phrase 'P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots' is slightly imprecise. The m·P quantity is the total useful work (m micro-batches × P stages), but the pipeline's total time is (m+P−1) stage-time units, not m·P. The P−1 extra time units are the bubble, but they are not 'wasted out of m·P slots'—they are added to the m useful time units to make m+P−1 total. A reader doing the arithmetic may be confused by the denominator framing.
evidence: For P=4, m=8: total time = 11 stage-units; useful work = 32 stage-units (8×4); bubble = 3 stage-units (P−1). The speedup is 32/11, not 32/(32−3). The 'P−1 out of m·P' framing conflates the time-domain bubble with the work-domain total.
root_cause: The explanation tries to give intuition for the denominator (m+P−1) by referencing the numerator (mP), but the 'wasted out of' phrasing implies a subtraction from mP rather than an addition to m.
correction: Rephrase to: 'the pipeline takes m+P−1 stage-time units to complete m·P units of useful work; the P−1 extra units are the fill-and-drain bubble. The ideal speedup over a single serial pass (m·P units) is therefore mP/(m+P−1).'
acceptance_test: A reader can verify the P=4, m=8 case: 11 time units for 32 useful units → speedup 32/11 ≈ 2.9, without needing to reconcile 'P−1 out of m·P' with the actual denominator.

page_hint: Ch 10, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second bullet (MoE scaling)
quoted_clause: Kimi K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE
observed: A reader doing the arithmetic gets 16/896 × 2.8T ≈ 50B, not 104B. The discrepancy is because 'active parameters' in MoE literature includes non-expert components (attention, shared layers, embeddings), but the text does not state this. The subsequent sentence '16/896 ≈ 1.8% expert activation' correctly refers to the expert routing fraction, but the juxtaposition with '104B active' without explanation invites confusion.
evidence: 16 × (2.8T / 896) = 16 × 3.125B = 50B (expert-only active). 104B − 50B = 54B (non-expert active: attention, shared FFN, embeddings, etc.). The text does not decompose this.
root_cause: The parenthetical '(2.8T total / 104B active)' uses the standard MoE 'active parameters' convention without flagging that it includes non-expert components, creating an apparent arithmetic inconsistency with the 16/896 routing ratio.
correction: Add a brief clause: '(2.8T total; 104B active, of which ~50B is the 16 routed experts and the remainder is attention and shared layers)'. Alternatively, rephrase to: 'activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token (≈1.8% expert activation; 2.8T total parameters, 104B active including non-expert components)'.
acceptance_test: A reader who computes 16/896 × 2.8T does not encounter an unexplained gap between the result (~50B) and the stated 'active' figure (104B).

page_hint: Ch 10 §2 (Mental Model), resource-triangle paragraph
quoted_clause: When a GPU is *idle* waiting, we reach for DP/CP (more work per GPU).
observed: The parenthetical mischaracterises sequence/context parallelism. CP does not give a GPU more work per token; it partitions the sequence so that a context too large for one GPU can be processed at all, at the cost of per-layer attention exchanges. Grouping CP with DP under 'more work per GPU' gives the reader the wrong reason to choose it, and the chapter's own Table 10-1 row for CP ('long contexts, KV too big') says otherwise.
evidence: Internal: Table 10-1 lists CP as splitting 'the token sequence' and fitting when 'long contexts, KV too big'; §1 item 5 says CP is 'useful for very long contexts where the KV cache or attention activations exceed one GPU'.
root_cause: The triangle's three corners (weights / activations / data) were mapped onto strategies, and CP was assigned to the 'data' corner because it also splits a dimension.
correction: Separate the two: 'When a GPU is idle waiting for work, we reach for DP (more requests per GPU). When a single sequence no longer fits one GPU, we reach for CP (split the sequence, pay per-layer attention exchanges).'
acceptance_test: The resource-triangle paragraph's parentheticals match the 'Fits when' column of Table 10-1 for every strategy it names.

page_hint: Ch 10 §4 item 3; compare Ch 13 §4 item 3
quoted_clause: For DP, time the gradient all-reduce as a fraction of step time — if it exceeds ~20%, it caps scaling.
observed: The same ~20% threshold appears in Ch 13 §4 with an evidence label ('>~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time on collectives') and in Ch 10 without one. The book's evidence taxonomy requires the label, and the inconsistency means a reader cannot tell whether Ch 10's threshold is a measured rule or a heuristic.
evidence: Cross-chapter: Ch 13 §4 item 3 labels the identical threshold; Ch 10 §4 item 3 and Ch 10 §8 mini-case ('stays under ~20% of step time') do not.
root_cause: The threshold was introduced in Ch 10 and later restated in Ch 13 with a label; the label was not back-ported.
correction: Add '[ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic]' to the Ch 10 §4 threshold and to the Ch 10 §8 mini-case restatement, matching Ch 13.
acceptance_test: The ~20% threshold carries the same evidence label in every chapter where it appears.

quoted_clause: There is also an inference-specific family — context/pipeline partitioning, expert parallelism, and P/D disaggregation
observed: The label 'inference-specific family' is applied to three strategies, but the same sentence immediately states that context/pipeline partitioning and expert parallelism 'both appear in training too.' Only P/D disaggregation is inference-specific.
evidence: The sentence reads: 'of the three, only P/D disaggregation has no training analogue (context/pipeline partitioning and expert parallelism both appear in training too).' The modifier contradicts 2 of 3 members within the same sentence.
root_cause: The family label asserts inference-specificity for strategies that also appear in training, creating an internal contradiction within one sentence.
correction: Reword to: 'There is also a serving-relevant family — context/pipeline partitioning, expert parallelism, and P/D disaggregation — repurposed here for serving; of the three, only P/D disaggregation has no training analogue.'
acceptance_test: The family label no longer asserts inference-specificity for strategies that also appear in training.

page_hint: Ch 10 §6, Table 10-1
quoted_clause: Table 10-1 above consolidates the five parallelization strategies (plus the serving-only P/D disaggregation)
observed: The text claims Table 10-1 includes P/D disaggregation, but the table has only 5 data rows (TP, PP, DP, EP, CP). P/D disaggregation is not present as a row.
evidence: Table 10-1 as printed contains exactly 5 rows: Tensor (TP), Pipeline (PP), Data (DP), Expert (EP), Sequence (CP). No P/D row exists. The colon after the parenthetical implies the table includes it.

page_hint: Ch 10 §1 item 6; Ch 11 §1 item 4; Ch 11 §4 item 3; Ch 12 §2
quoted_clause: separates the compute-bound prefill stage from the bandwidth-bound decode stage onto different GPU pools ... splitting the compute-bound *prefill* stage from the bandwidth-bound *decode* stage onto separate pools, because they bottleneck on different resources ... a FLOP-bound prefill core and a bandwidth-bound decode core running on one pool tells us when to disaggregate ... compute (prefill throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidth-bound)
observed: In four places the prefill/decode regime split is stated as an unqualified property of the phases rather than as a first-order regime whose validity depends on sequence length, batch size, precision, kernels and hardware. The book's own numbers show the regime is workload-dependent (a 9.2K-token prefill on the canonical 8-GPU host is compute-heavy, but a short-prompt, large-batch decode step can be compute-heavy too, and a large-batch prefill can become memory-bound on activations). A reader can carry away 'prefill is always compute-bound, decode is always bandwidth-bound' as a law, which is exactly the inference the book elsewhere warns against.
evidence: Internal: Ch 11 §3's own figures are regime-specific (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 peak for a single device; 5.6 TB/s vs 0.70 TB/s per GPU for decode) and are stated without the conditions that make them true; Ch 12 §3's 19.8K tok/s prefill ceiling is an MFU-based aggregate that already embeds a batch-size assumption.
root_cause: A useful first-order heuristic has been promoted to a definitional statement at each point of use, without a single place where the regime conditions are stated once and referenced thereafter.
correction: State the regime once with its conditions (e.g. 'at long prompt lengths and modest batch, prefill is compute-bound; at small batch and short prompts, decode is bandwidth-bound; both regimes move with batch size, precision and kernel efficiency — see Ch 6 for the crossover arithmetic') and reference it at each of the four sites. Where a specific canonical number is quoted, keep the number and add the condition that produced it.
acceptance_test: Each of the four sites either carries an explicit regime qualifier or points to a single place where the qualifier is stated; no sentence in Chs 10–12 asserts the compute-bound/bandwidth-bound split without a scope.

quoted_clause: *Ornith-1.5-397B* (released 2026-08-19 by DeepReinforce / `ornith-ai`) ships as another natively multimodal frontier model: 397 B MoE, ~262 K context, MIT weights, image-input via the inherited Qwen3.5 vision tower.

The appendix's own footnote cites https://ornith.ai/ornith_1_5.html, which is the place to check.

root_cause: Unverified — the parameter count may be correct for the cited variant, or the book may carry two different figures for the same family.

page_hint: Ch 11 §6 (Architecture Consequence, 'Baseline' bullet); contradicted in Ch 12 §3 and Ch 13 §3; correct framing present in Ch 11 §8 and Ch 14 §3 Step 3
quoted_clause: **Baseline (canonical single-host):** continuous batching (vLLM/Orca) is near-mandatory to hold TTFT under the SLO (1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s) at 10 rps input-heavy load
observed: The baseline bullet asserts that a single canonical 8×H100 host holds the TTFT SLO at 10 rps. Ch 12 §3 states the same host sustains only ~19,800 prefill tok/s against a ~92K input tok/s demand at 10 rps (4.65× short), and Ch 13 §3 explicitly says the single host is 'latency-feasible but not capacity-sufficient'. Ch 11's own mini-case uses the correct framing ('that replica's assigned load'), and Ch 14 Step 3 uses an offered load of 1.3 req/s. As written, a reader can conclude that one host serves the canonical average load at SLO — a decision-relevant contradiction between adjacent chapters.
evidence: Recomputation: 10 rps × 9,200 input tok = 92,000 tok/s demand; 8 × 2,472 = 19,776 tok/s host prefill ceiling → 4.65× shortfall (Ch 12's own figure). Ch 13's per-host residency ceiling 17 ÷ 8.6 ≈ 1.98 rps vs 10 rps offered. Both are the book's numbers, not mine.
root_cause: The §6 bullet conflates per-request latency feasibility with aggregate capacity at a stated arrival rate. The necessary qualifier exists in Ch 11 §8 and Ch 13 §3 but was not carried into the chapter's headline architecture-consequence bullet.
correction: Split the claim: (a) continuous batching is required to hold TTFT at the host's *admitted* operating point (≈1.3–2 req/s per Ch 14 Step 3 and the 17/8.6 ≈ 1.98 rps ceiling); (b) at the canonical 10 rps average the host class must be replicated ~5–6× (Ch 12/17), and continuous batching is what keeps each replica's tail inside the SLO. Remove 'at 10 rps input-heavy load' from the single-host clause or replace it with 'at the replica's admitted load'.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 11 §6 asserts that one 8×H100 host meets the TTFT SLO at 10 rps. A cross-read of Ch 11 §6, Ch 12 §3 (19.8K vs 92K) and Ch 13 §3 (1.98 rps/host) yields no apparent contradiction; the phrase 'per-request latency' and 'aggregate capacity' are used distinctly wherever the 10 rps figure appears.

page_hint: Ch 11, §3 Worked Example, 'When to Disaggregate' subsection, first sentence of the P/D paragraph
quoted_clause: prefill is compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak), decode is bandwidth-bound (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU
observed: The prefill figure (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak) shows a single H100 cannot meet the prefill budget, which is correct. However, the text does not explicitly state the consequence: that the 8×H100 host (7.912 PFLOPS aggregate) has ~6.6× headroom for prefill, and the binding constraint for prefill on the canonical host is not raw FLOPS but the scheduling/batching interaction with decode. As written, a reader might conclude that prefill is 'infeasible' on a single H100 (true) but miss that the 8-GPU host is comfortably in the compute-bound regime for prefill and the real P/D tension is the scheduling conflict, not a raw capacity shortfall.
evidence: 8 × 0.989 = 7.912 PFLOPS aggregate. Required: 1.19 PFLOPS. Ratio: 6.6×. The text states the per-device numbers but does not close the loop to the 8-device host that is the canonical baseline.
root_cause: The per-device comparison is correct but the architectural consequence for the canonical 8×H100 host is left implicit, weakening the 'why disaggregate' argument at the scale where it actually matters (multi-node, not single-host).
correction: After the per-device numbers, add one sentence: 'On the canonical 8×H100 host the aggregate prefill capacity (≈7.9 PFLOPS) exceeds the 1.19 PFLOPS requirement by a wide margin; the P/D tension on a single host is a scheduling conflict (batching for prefill inflates decode latency), not a raw FLOPS shortfall. The raw-capacity argument becomes binding only when the workload outgrows one node and the two phases must be placed on separate, independently sized pools.'
acceptance_test: A reader can distinguish (a) the single-GPU infeasibility that motivates TP, from (b) the scheduling conflict that motivates P/D on a single host, from (c) the independent-sizing benefit that motivates P/D at multi-node scale.

page_hint: Ch 11 §3 ('When to Disaggregate' paragraph) and Fig 11.3 caption; reconciled by Ch 12 §3
quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak), decode is **bandwidth-bound** (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU; under the canonical 8×H100 host it is sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU)
observed: The prefill feasibility comparison is a single-device comparison (1.19 PFLOPS required vs one H100's 0.989 PFLOPS peak) presented in a chapter whose canonical deployment is an 8×H100 host with TP=8. Under that deployment the same 1.29 PFLOP prefill is 0.161 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at the book's own 35% MFU — comfortably inside the ~1.08 s budget. The prose does not say 'single device', so a reader can conclude the canonical host cannot meet the prefill budget, which contradicts Ch 12's per-host prefill rate of ~19,800 tok/s (9,200 tokens in ~0.47 s). The Fig 11.3 caption does say 'single-H100'; the prose does not.
evidence: Recomputation: 1.288e15 FLOP ÷ 8 GPUs = 1.61e14 FLOP/GPU; at 989 TFLOP/s × 35% = 346.15 TFLOP/s → 0.465 s. Ch 12's 19,776 tok/s ÷ 9,200 tok = 0.465 s — the same number, confirming the canonical host meets the prefill budget. The printed 1.19 PFLOPS figure is correct only for a single device.
root_cause: A single-device feasibility check was carried over from the single-host framing of earlier chapters into a multi-GPU canonical context without re-scoping the denominator.
correction: Add 'on a single device' to the prose and add the canonical reconciliation in the same sentence: '…vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak on one H100; under the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 host the same prefill is ~0.16 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (Ch 12), so the single-device figure describes a one-GPU deployment, not the canonical host.'
acceptance_test: Every prefill-feasibility statement in Ch 11 names the device count it assumes; the 1.19 PFLOPS figure is never presented as a property of the canonical 8-GPU host.

page_hint: Ch 11 §4 (block headed 'Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability'); Ch 11 §6 (block headed 'The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically')
quoted_clause: ### Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability ... ### The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically
observed: Two substantial digressions are placed under headings whose intellectual job they do not perform. The §4 block (hybrid models, looped-depth models, adaptive depth, depth-aware latency, economic denominator) sits inside 'Measurement' but is a capability-qualification argument, not a measurement protocol. The §6 block (Wan2.2, VAE reconstruction, CFG, Ulysses, FSDP, video admission records) sits inside 'Architecture Consequence' but is a transfer note about a different media domain; it introduces a large new vocabulary (VAE, CFG, Ulysses, timestep schedules) in a chapter about LLM serving, and it is the last thing a reader meets before the mini-case. Together these blocks are roughly a third of the chapter's prose, and neither is signposted in the chapter's opening promise ('how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode').
evidence: Structural: the chapter's stated scope in 'The Architect's Question' lists four mechanisms; the qualification and video blocks address none of them. The video block's own content is explicitly about a different workload class ('A text prefill/decode split does not prove that the same split is useful here').
root_cause: Two later additions (model-capability qualification and non-text transfer) were inserted into whichever section was open rather than being given their own signposted place in the chapter's argument.
correction: Give each block its own numbered subsection with a title that states its job — e.g. §4.x 'Capability qualification is not serving capability' (moved out of Measurement) and §6.x 'Transfer: the serving concerns transfer, the mechanisms do not' — and add one sentence to the chapter's opening promise acknowledging them. Consider moving the video material to an appendix if the chapter is to stay within its stated scope, keeping only the two-paragraph principle in the body.
acceptance_test: Every subsection in Ch 11 has a heading whose claim matches the subsection's content; the chapter's opening promise enumerates the subsections it contains; a reader who reads only the chapter's own promise can predict its subsections.

page_hint: Ch 11 Table 11-2 and its surrounding text; Ch 11 §6 footnotes oct-ix-openvino-paged-attention and oct-ix-sglang-xpu-graph
quoted_clause: #### Table 11-2 — Serving engines by architectural capability (time-sensitive) ... | supported hardware | NVIDIA / AMD / CPU | NVIDIA / AMD | NVIDIA-only | CPU + consumer GPUs | deployment niche |
observed: Two defects in the book's most explicitly time-sensitive table. (1) It carries no observation date, although the book dates every other implementation snapshot (Table 9-3 '(2026-10-28 snapshot)', the 'Dated implementation note', the OpenVINO and SGLang XPU footnotes all dated 2026-10-28) and the text itself says the rows 'must be re-verified against each engine's current first-party documentation'. (2) The 'supported hardware' row omits Intel XPU for both vLLM and SGLang, even though this same chapter's footnotes document a vLLM XPU platform source and SGLang XPU documentation — the table contradicts the chapter's own evidence.
evidence: Internal: Ch 11 §6 cites 'vLLM XPU platform source, pinned to revision 5df63a7' and 'SGLang XPU documentation at pinned revision a1966e1', and §4 discusses the vLLM XPU configuration selecting the XCCL backend. Table 11-2's supported-hardware row lists no Intel entry for either engine.

Add Intel XPU to the supported-hardware cells for vLLM and SGLang (or replace the cell with 'NVIDIA / AMD / Intel XPU / CPU' as observed), and add a 'not observed' marker convention so that absence of evidence is distinguishable from absence of support.

page_hint: Ch 11 §6, 'Baseline (canonical single-host)' bullet
quoted_clause: PagedAttention ensures the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV pack fits

page_hint: Ch 11 §3, Prefix Caching paragraph
observed: The symbol K is invoked without definition at the point of use, and the arithmetic that follows ('1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200') does not involve K at all. A reader who has not met K in the FLOP model cannot tell what it scales, and the parenthetical as written does not explain the 1.12 PFLOP figure it sits inside.
evidence: The sentence's own arithmetic (1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200) is a token-count decomposition, unrelated to a scaling constant K; the FLOP figure 2 × 70e9 × 8,000 = 1.12e15 is derived from the 8,000-token prefix alone.
root_cause: A cross-reference to a symbol defined in another chapter was inserted mid-sentence without the definition or a pointer.
correction: Either define K inline ('K = 1,000 is the book's token-scaling constant for the FLOP model, Ch 6') or remove the reference and state the derivation directly: '2 × 70 × 10⁹ FLOP/token × 8,000 tokens ≈ 1.12 PFLOP for the shared prefix; the full 9,200-token input is ~1.29 PFLOP'.
acceptance_test: Every symbol used in a derivation in Ch 11 is defined at or before first use, or carries an explicit chapter pointer.
